opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, when I first started thinking seriously about it, during my PhD, I was pretty skeptical that pure reinforcement learning would get us to something like cooking a meal anytime soon. Not because RL isn't powerful. We'd all seen what it could do in games, in Go and Atari. But those settings share some properties that the real world just doesn't give you.

The first issue is sample efficiency. RL learns by trial and error, often millions of trials. In simulation that's fine; you can run thousands of copies in parallel. But a real robot in a real kitchen breaks things, spills things, and runs at real-world speed. You can't reset the environment by pressing a button. Someone has to clean up the mess and put the eggs back. That alone makes naive scaling very hard.

The second issue is the reward. In a game you have a score. In cooking, what's the reward? "Make a good omelet" is incredibly hard to specify as a number. If you try to hand-engineer it, the robot finds some weird shortcut you didn't anticipate. If you make it sparse, like "one if the meal is done," the robot will basically never stumble onto that by random exploration, because a meal is a long sequence of steps: get the pan, crack the eggs, whisk, control the heat. The search space is astronomically large.

So the way I assessed it was: the real bottleneck isn't the optimization algorithm, it's the structure and the data. Long-horizon tasks like cooking are compositional. They're made of reusable skills, grasping, pouring, stirring, and higher-level reasoning about what to do next. That pushed me toward two directions. One was hierarchical approaches, where you separate high-level task planning from low-level motor skills, so you're not learning everything from scratch end to end. The other was learning from demonstrations, imitation learning, because humans already know how to cook. If we can show the robot, collect good data at scale, we skip a huge amount of blind exploration.

I don't think RL goes away. I think it becomes the fine-tuning layer. You get a reasonable policy from human data or from a pretrained model, and then RL helps the robot refine, recover from mistakes, and get more robust. That combination feels much more scalable to me than asking a robot to discover cooking from zero.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So, I'd say I'm optimistic about scaling RL for robots, but my optimism is pretty conditional on where the scaling actually happens.

The honest assessment is that pure reinforcement learning, in the sense of a robot exploring from scratch in the real world and getting a reward when the pasta turns out right, does not scale to something like cooking a meal. Cooking is a long-horizon task. It's dozens of sub-steps, each of which can fail in ways that compound. The reward is sparse and delayed, the state space is enormous, and real-world interaction is slow and expensive. If you need millions of trials for a single manipulation skill, you're not going to get a full meal that way. Hardware breaks, kitchens aren't resettable, and nobody wants to clean up ten thousand failed attempts at cracking an egg.

So the way I've thought about it is that RL shouldn't be the thing that discovers the structure of the task. The structure should come from somewhere else. That's a big part of why I spent so much time on learning from demonstrations and on hierarchical approaches. A human can show you what cooking looks like in a handful of examples. That gives you the task decomposition, the rough sequence of skills, the "what should happen next." RL then becomes a refinement tool. It's good at the local stuff: adjusting a grasp, recovering when the spatula slips, tightening up a policy that was initialized from demonstration data. In that regime the horizon is short, the reward is dense, and the sample complexity is actually manageable.

The other thing that changed my assessment, and I think a lot of people's, is the arrival of large pretrained models. A few years ago the bottleneck for everyday tasks was that the robot had no common-sense understanding of a kitchen at all. Now you can get a reasonable high-level plan, "get the pan, turn on the stove, add oil," essentially for free from a language or vision-language model. That takes a lot of pressure off RL. You're no longer asking it to learn semantics, you're asking it to ground an already-reasonable plan in physical behavior. That's a much better division of labor.

Where I remain skeptical is in anything that pretends the real world is a simulator. Sim-to-real has made real progress for locomotion and some rigid-object manipulation, but cooking involves deformables, liquids, heat, things that are genuinely hard to simulate well. So the scaling story there has to lean on real data, on demonstrations, and on being clever about how little RL you actually need.

So, to sum it up: I don't think we scale RL to cooking by scaling RL. We scale it by giving the robot enough prior structure, from humans and from pretrained models, that RL is only asked to solve the parts it's actually good at. That's a much more tractable problem, and I think it's the one worth betting on.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is what we actually need to scale. With reinforcement learning, a robot needs to try things, get feedback, and improve. But for something like cooking a meal, collecting that experience in the real world is slow. Mistakes can break things, and someone has to reset the kitchen before the robot can try again.

Cooking also involves a long sequence of decisions. If the meal turns out badly, how do you figure out which action caused the problem? Was it how you handled an ingredient, the timing, or something much earlier? That makes learning from a final success or failure signal very difficult.

So I would assess the prospect by asking whether we can make the learning process more efficient: start from demonstrations, practice in simulation where it helps, and use real-world interaction to refine those skills. Reinforcement learning can be an important part of that, but scaling it means solving the data collection and feedback problems, not just running a larger algorithm.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first question is what we mean by scaling. In simulation, you can run many copies of a robot and collect experience in parallel. But for something like cooking a meal, the challenge is getting that experience to translate to a real kitchen, where objects, ingredients, and conditions keep changing.

There’s also the question of feedback. Did the robot successfully cook the meal? That’s a very delayed signal if it made a mistake ten minutes earlier. You need a way to learn the smaller skills, combine them, and recover when something goes wrong.

So I’d assess the prospect by looking at whether more training produces reliable improvements across different situations, rather than just better performance on one setup. I think reinforcement learning can be an important part of that, especially for refining skills through interaction, but the practical path likely combines it with demonstrations and prior knowledge. The goal is to make each real-world interaction more useful, because collecting robot experience is expensive.
